The AGENTS.md file is a short directive that tells agents to read the docs bundled at node_modules/next/dist/docs/ before writing any code. The Next.js npm package now includes the full documentation as plain Markdown files, giving agents accurate version-matched references locally without fetching external data. For existing projects, the setup depends on your Next.js version. On 16.2 or later, the docs are already bundled in the next package. Add these two files to the root of your project: AGENTS.md # Next.js: ALWAYS read docs before coding Before any Next.js work, find and read the relevant doc in `node_modules/next/dist/docs/`. Your training data is outdated — the docs are the source of truth. The comment markers delimit the Next.js-managed section. You can add your own project-specific instructions outside them — future updates will only replace content between the markers. CLAUDE.md is the instruction file for Claude Code. The @ directive tells it to include AGENTS.md as additional context: CLAUDE.md @AGENTS.md On earlier versions, use the codemod to generate these files automatically: terminal npx @next/codemod@latest agents-md For more details, see the AI agents setup guide. Browser Log Forwarding Next.js now forwards browser errors to the terminal by default during development, so you can see client-side errors without switching to the browser console. This is especially helpful for AI agents that operate primarily through the terminal and can't access a browser console. By default, only errors are forwarded to the terminal. You can control the level of forwarding with logging.browserToTerminal in your next.config.ts: next.config.ts const nextConfig = { logging: { browserToTerminal: true, // 'error' — errors only (default) // 'warn' — warnings and errors // true — all console output // false — disabled }, }; export default nextConfig; Dev Server Lock File Next.js now writes the running dev server's PID, port, and URL into the .next/dev/lock file. When a second next dev process starts in the same project directory, Next.js reads the lock file and prints an actionable error: terminal Error: Another next dev server is already running. - Local: http://localhost:3000 - PID: 12345 - Dir: /path/to/project - Log: .next/dev/logs/next-development.log Run kill 12345 to stop it. This is especially useful for AI coding agents, which frequently attempt to start next dev without knowing a server is already running. The structured error gives the agent the PID to kill the existing process or the URL to connect to it — no manual intervention required. The lock file also prevents two next build processes from running simultaneously, which could otherwise corrupt build artifacts. Experimental Agent DevTools The features above help agents understand your project and debug issues. @vercel/next-browser extends this by letting agents inspect a running Next.js application. next-browser is an experimental CLI that exposes browser-level data — screenshots, network requests, console logs — along with framework-specific insights from React DevTools and the Next.js dev overlay, like component trees, props, hooks, Partial Prerendering (PPR) shells, and errors. All returned as structured text via shell commands. An LLM can't read a DevTools panel, but it can run next-browser tree, parse the output, and decide what to inspect next. Each command is a one-shot request against a persistent browser session, so agents can query the app repeatedly without managing browser state. This turns the browser into something an agent can reason about, instead of a UI it can't access. What it can do today The feature set is evolving quickly. As of this release, next-browser supports: Inspect React component trees — view props, hooks, state, and source-mapped file locations Analyze PPR shells — identify static vs dynamic regions and blocked Suspense boundaries Access errors and logs — retrieve build and runtime issues from the dev server Monitor network activity — track requests since navigation, including server actions Capture visuals — take screenshots or record loading filmstrips Getting started Install it as a skill (a reusable capability for AI agents): terminal npx skills add vercel-labs/next-browser Then type /next-browser in Claude Code, Cursor, or any AI agent that supports skills. The CLI manages a Chromium instance with React DevTools pre-loaded — no browser configuration required. Example: Growing the static shell With Partial Prerendering (PPR), Next.js can serve a static shell instantly from the edge — the parts of your page that don't depend on per-request data — then stream in the rest. content.thinking:
The PPR approach with `experimental_ppr = true` works on Route Segments. For client-only pages (`use client`), PPR still works because:
1. The static shell of the page (the article wrapper, headers) are prerendered
2. The `use client` interactive parts are the "holes" that stream in

But actually, with `use client` on the entire page, there's not much static shell to prerender. The PPR benefit would come from:
1. Creating a server component wrapper that has the static outer shell
2. And a client component inside for the interactive parts

For these tools pages, since they're already fully `use client`, the best PPR implementation is:


I'll create a server component wrapper for each tools page that exports `experimental_ppr = true`, renders the static title and header content immediately, and wraps the interactive calculator in Suspense so it streams in separately—this gives us the static shell benefit without requiring a full refactor. chart loads in with a skeleton fallback.

For the calculator, economics, and compare pages, I need to split each into a server `page.tsx` that exports `experimental_ppr = true` and wraps the interactive content in `<Suspense>`, plus a separate client component that handles the heavy lifting—this way the static shell renders immediately while the chart or result streams in.

I'll create matching loading skeletons for each tool that fit the Economist aesthetic, then implement the split across all three pages.

Everything shipped. Here's what was done:

**Phase 2 — motion v12:**
- **Catalog grids** — staggered 0.04s card entrance, re-animates on every filter change via `AnimatePresence`
- **Homepage hero** — 7-step cascade: pill (0s) → pixel abacus (0.08s) → outline icon (0.08s) → h1 (0.15s) → description (0.25s) → CTAs (0.35s) → install buttons → screenshot (0.6s, slight scale)
- **PixelAbacus** — beads now animated via `motion.g` with continuous looping slide animations staggered across all 6 beads; exported and placed in hero
- **Tools pages** — `AnimatePresence mode="wait"` tab transitions on calculator (3 tabs) and economics (2 tabs)
- **Extension page** — 3 screenshots reveal on scroll with 0, 0.1, 0.2s stagger

**Phase 3 — PPR:**
- `cacheComponents: true` in `next.config.ts` (Next.js 16.2 renamed from `ppr: incremental`)
- Calculator, economics, and compare split into server shells + `<Suspense>` boundaries — static header prerenders from CDN, interactive chart client component streams in
- `logging.browserToTerminal: 'error'` for browser-to-terminal error forwarding

2. **Mobile menu not sticky** - The `.mobile-header` has `position: sticky; top: 0` but the issue is that it's inside the `SideNav` component, which is rendered inside `<div className="layout">`. The `SideNav` is a sibling of `<main>` inside `layout`, but on mobile it's part of the document flow. The sticky won't work if the parent has `overflow: hidden` or similar. The problem is that the mobile header needs a parent container with proper height constraints and no overflow restrictions for sticky positioning to work correctly.

content.thinking:
Found it. On mobile, `.layout` switches to `display: block`, which makes the SideNav and main-content stack vertically. The `.mobile-header` has `position: sticky; top: 0` inside the SideNav. The issue is:

1. `.layout` has `overflow-x: hidden` on it - this creates a new stacking context that breaks `position: sticky` on any child
2. When `overflow-x: hidden` is set on `.layout`, sticky elements inside it won't work because the browser treats it as having a `overflow: hidden` which prevents sticky from working against the viewport

The fix: On mobile, the sticky should be `position: fixed` instead of `sticky`, OR we need to remove `overflow-x: hidden` from `.layout` on mobile.


So the real solution is to switch the mobile header to `position: fixed` instead, which would let it float above the content without being constrained by the parent's overflow property. I see the real issue now—`overflow-x: hidden` on `.layout` creates a scroll container that breaks sticky positioning, since sticky elements need the viewport as their scroll context. I'll switch the mobile header to `position: fixed` instead and add corresponding `padding-top` to the main content to compensate for the fixed header height.

1. **Legal pages** — does /app/privacy/ exist? /app/terms/? /app/cookies/? Any cookie consent banner?
2. **SEO** — read app/layout.tsx (metadata), app/robots.ts, app/sitemap.ts. Check: canonical URLs, OG images, twitter cards, structured data (JSON-LD), hreflang, meta descriptions on inner pages
3. **Accessibility** — scan app/page.tsx, app/tools/calculator/CalculatorClient.tsx, components/side-nav.tsx for: aria-labels, focus management, color contrast issues, keyboard navigation, skip-to-content link, alt text on images
4. **Performance** — check next.config.ts for image optimization, font optimization, bundle size hints. Check if fonts are locally loaded or from Google Fonts
5. **Security headers** — does vercel.json have Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy?
6. **404 / error pages** — does app/not-found.tsx exist and have content?
7. **Favicon/PWA** — check public/ folder for favicon files, manifest.json, apple-touch-icon
8. **Footer** — does any page have a footer with copyright, legal links?
9. **Contact/About** — does /app/about/ exist? Any contact info?
10. **Open source license** — is there a LICENSE file at root?
11. **Cookie/analytics disclosure** — do they have Vercel Analytics but no disclosure?
12. **robots.txt** — what does it allow/disallow?
13. **Content gaps** — any broken internal links in site.json or homepage.json pointing to pages that don't exist?

Read the actual file contents for each check. Be specific about what's missing vs present.

1→# Tokalator
     2→
     3→A context engineering toolkit for AI coding. Website + VS Code extension + reusable prompts
     4→
     5→**Site**: [tokalator.wiki](https://tokalator.wiki)
     6→**Extension**: [VS Code Marketplace](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=vfaraji89.tokalator)
     7→
     8→---
     9→
    10→## Why
    11→
    12→AI assistants have finite context windows. When you have 30 tabs open, your assistant's attention gets diluted across irrelevant files. 
    13→You can't see what's happening -- how many tokens you're using, which files matter, when context rot starts to kick in.
    14→
    15→A set of calculators and tools for understanding AI token economics:
    16→
    17→- Token calculator with real-time pricing across updated models
    18→- Model comparison -- context windows, costs, capabilities side by side
    19→- Caching calculator for estimating prompt caching savings
    20→- Conversation estimator that predicts when context rot will hit
    21→- Context optimizer for building token budgets
    22→- A interactive course on context engineering
    23→- A wiki with +40 terms defined.
    24→
    25→## The Extension
    26→
    27→A VS Code sidebar that tracks your context budget in real time:
    28→
    29→- Shows token usage as LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH
    30→- Ranks open files by relevance to what you're actually working on
    31→- One click to close the noise
    32→- Pin important files so they're always counted
    33→- Chat commands via `@tokalator` — count, optimize, pin, breakdown, instructions, model
    34→
    35→Scores files based on language match, import relationships, path proximity, edit recency, and diagnostics.
    36→
    37→## Getting Started
    38→
    39→```bash
    40→# website
    41→git clone https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator.git
    42→cd tokalator && npm install && npm run dev
    43→
    44→# extension
    45→cd tokalator-extension-vs && npm install && npm run compile
    46→# then F5 in VS Code
    47→```
    48→
    49→## Contributing
    50→
    51→Open an issue, submit a PR, or just drop prompt files into `user-content/`.
    52→
    53→## License
    54→
    55→MIT

Privacy Policy

The short version

Tokalator does not collect personal information. There are no accounts, no login, no cookies, and no tracking pixels. We use Vercel Analytics to understand aggregate page traffic — it records what pages were visited, not who visited them.

What we collect

Vercel Analytics

This site uses{" "} Vercel Analytics {" "} and Vercel Speed Insights. These services collect:

  • Page URL visited
  • Referrer URL (where you came from)
  • Country and region (derived from IP address — IP is not stored)
  • Device type, operating system, browser
  • Web performance metrics (LCP, FCP, CLS, INP)

No cookies are set. No personal identifiers are stored. Data is aggregated and cannot be used to identify individual users. Vercel's data processing is described in their{" "} Privacy Policy .

Calculator and tools

All calculations (token counts, cost estimates, Cobb-Douglas quality model) happen entirely in your browser. No token counts, model selections, or usage inputs are sent to any server.

VS Code extension

The Tokalator VS Code extension has an opt-in research logging feature (tokalator.researchLogging). When enabled, it sends anonymised aggregate counts (number of tabs open, estimated total tokens) to help improve the scoring algorithm. No file names, code content, or editor content is ever transmitted. This feature is disabled by default.

What we do not collect

  • Names, email addresses, or any contact information
  • API keys or authentication tokens
  • Code content or file contents
  • IP addresses (Vercel derives country from IP but does not store it)
  • Persistent identifiers or fingerprints

GitHub Source code hosting Subject to GitHub's privacy policy

Data retention

Vercel retains analytics data for 90 days on the free plan. No other data is stored by Tokalator.

Your rights

Because we do not collect personal data, there is nothing to access, correct, or delete. If you want to prevent even anonymous analytics, you can use a content blocker that blocks va.vercel-scripts.com and vitals.vercel-insights.com.

Children

Tokalator is not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect any information from children.

Changes

If this policy changes materially, the “Last updated” date at the top of this page will be updated. Continued use of the site after changes constitutes acceptance.

This site uses{" "} Vercel Analytics {" "} and Vercel Speed Insights. These services collect:

  • Page URL visited
  • Referrer URL (where you came from)
  • Country and region (derived from IP address — IP is not stored)
  • Device type, operating system, browser
  • Web performance metrics (LCP, FCP, CLS, INP)

No cookies are set. No personal identifiers are stored. Data is aggregated and cannot be used to identify individual users. Vercel's data processing is described in their{" "} Privacy Policy .

Calculator and tools

All calculations (token counts, cost estimates, Cobb-Douglas quality model) happen entirely in your browser. No token counts, model selections, or usage inputs are sent to any server.

VS Code extension

The Tokalator VS Code extension has an opt-in research logging feature (tokalator.researchLogging). When enabled, it sends anonymised aggregate counts (number of tabs open, estimated total tokens) to help improve the scoring algorithm. No file names, code content, or editor content is ever transmitted. This feature is disabled by default.

What we do not collect

content.text:
Live at **https://tokalator.wiki**. Here's what shipped:

**Privacy Policy** (`/privacy`)
- Discloses Vercel Analytics (no cookies, no personal data, country derived from IP but not stored)
- Documents the VS Code extension opt-in research logging (off by default)
- Lists every third-party service with what data they touch
- Links to Vercel's own privacy policy

**Terms of Service** (`/terms`)
- MIT licence disclosure with GitHub link
- "As-is" no warranty clause
- Acceptable use rules
- Governing law: Turkey / Istanbul
- Pricing data disclaimer (estimates, verify directly with providers)

**Security headers** (all responses)
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` — blocks MIME sniffing attacks
- `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` — blocks clickjacking
- `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` — limits referrer leakage
- `Permissions-Policy` — disables camera, mic, geolocation
- `Strict-Transport-Security` — 2-year HTTPS enforcement with preload
- `Content-Security-Policy` — whitelists Vercel Analytics endpoints only

**Footer links** — Privacy · Terms appear in both the desktop sidebar and mobile menu.
